title: Occurrence, Preparation, and Properties of Halogens
lead: The halogens, fluorine to astatine, are too reactive to be found free in nature. The section follows how each is obtained from its halide ions, how strongly each acts as an oxidizing agent, how the halides of the representative metals and the interhalogens are prepared, and what the halogens are used for.
objectives: Describe the preparation, properties, and uses of halogens
Describe the properties, preparation, and uses of halogen compounds
summary_html:
The halogens form halides with less electronegative elements. Halides of the metals vary from ionic to covalent; halides of nonmetals are covalent. Interhalogens form by the combination of two or more different halogens.

All of the representative metals react directly with elemental halogens or with solutions of the hydrohalic acids (HF, HCl, HBr, and HI) to produce representative metal halides. Other laboratory preparations involve the addition of aqueous hydrohalic acids to compounds that contain such basic anions, such as hydroxides, oxides, or carbonates.

exercises.prompt: What does it mean to say that mercury(II) halides are weak electrolytes?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: recall what a weak electrolyte does when it dissolves, ionizing only partly so that most of it stays as molecules, and connect that with the text’s statement that mercury forms covalent rather than ionic binary halides; then say what dissolved HgCl<sub>2</sub> mostly consists of and how well its solution conducts electricity.

exercises.prompt: Why is SnCl<sub>4</sub> not classified as a salt?

answer.solution: SnCl<sub>4</sub> is not a salt because it is covalently bonded. A salt must have ionic bonds.

exercises.prompt: Which is the stronger acid, HClO<sub>3</sub> or HBrO<sub>3</sub>? Why?

answer.solution: In oxyacids with similar formulas, the acid strength increases as the electronegativity of the central atom increases. HClO<sub>3</sub> is stronger than HBrO<sub>3</sub>; Cl is more electronegative than Br.

exercises.prompt: Which halogen has the highest ionization energy? Is this what you would predict based on what you have learned about periodic properties?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: recall the trend in first ionization energy down a group from the chapter on electronic structure and periodic properties, where the valence electrons lie farther from the nucleus in each heavier element; then compare that prediction with the text’s statement that fluoride is the most difficult halide ion to oxidize and fluorine the most powerful oxidizing agent.

exercises.prompt:
Name each of the following compounds:
(a) BrF3
(b) NaBrO3
(c) PBr5
(d) NaClO4
(e) KClO

answer.solution: (a) bromine trifluoride; (b) sodium bromate; (c) phosphorus pentabromide; (d) sodium perchlorate; (e) potassium hypochlorite

exercises.prompt: Explain why, at room temperature, fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, and iodine is a solid.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: the four halogens are nonpolar diatomic molecules, so the only forces between their molecules are dispersion forces. Compare the numbers of electrons and the sizes of F<sub>2</sub>, Cl<sub>2</sub>, Br<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub>, say how the strength of the dispersion forces changes from one to the next, and connect that with how high the melting and boiling points must be.
